title: Embeddings as Relational Meaning — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Embeddings as Relational Meaning’s rich face, its first round, a Study and still a proposal: two walks on real GloVe vectors that each start from one idea and end on a test of the page’s own claim (does a direction carry a relation, beyond what nearness alone gives; are categories regions, and is the page’s musical-interval region about intervals). I lean where the page leans: demonstrations that make the relational claim testable. I grow when the page is enriched again; I never hold the entry’s words.
grain: The page’s own ## grain: the opening (the H1 section) and The Geometry of Meaning each carry one piece. Origin, Cross-Pillar Connections and Open Questions carry none: nothing there a piece could test without forcing it.

offers.what: “king − man + woman ≈ queen” holds only when the three input words are left out of the answers. With them in, the nearest word to the tip is king itself (GloVe 100-d: king 0.836, queen 0.770 over the piece’s 3,146 words; king first over all 341,479 too). The example also comes from static embeddings (word2vec, Mikolov et al. 2013), while the paragraph opens “In large language models”. The claim behind it holds: across 3,448 word2vec analogy quads the page doesn’t state, the arrow b − a + c lands on d first 84.3% of the time, against 44.4% for a reader who only looks near c and 0.0% for shuffled vectors. Over the 100,000 most frequent words it is 80.6% against 35.8%. Offer: “(king − man + woman ≈ queen, once the three input words are set aside)”, and name the example as word2vec’s.

The section’s own example, “musical intervals”, is a region that static vectors can’t keep clean. Six of its interval names are also ordinals, and in GloVe 100-d all six (third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, ninth) sit nearer plain ordinals that name no interval (first, twentieth, thirtieth, fortieth, hundredth: 0.50 to 0.58) than the interval names that aren’t ordinals (unison, semitone, tone, tritone, octave, interval: 0.21 to 0.27). The control arm (those six names, plus chord, pitch, melody) sits on the interval side 9 of 9. Fifth’s eight nearest words are all ordinals. The regions themselves are real (35 of 36 by leave-one-out, against 14 of 36 shuffled, chance 12). Offer: one sentence in the second paragraph saying the bank problem lives inside the first paragraph’s example too. In a static embedding, fifth the interval and fifth the place in a race are one point, and the race wins. That is the case for context the page already makes, in its own domain.

pieces.title: directions · a walk in five steps
pieces.caption: **Does a direction carry a relation?** Two words and the angle between them, a word’s neighbours, a relation as an arrow, the page’s own sum (shown, not scored), and last a test on 3,448 word2vec analogy quads the page never states: does b − a + c land on d more often than a reader who only looks near c? Chance, the rule and both controls are stated before the run. Real vectors: 3,146 words of the npm package wink-embeddings-sg-100d 1.1.0 (MIT, GRAYPE Systems), derived from Stanford GloVe pre-trained vectors (PDDL 1.0), inlined. GloVe’s numbers: static, 100 dimensions, not a transformer’s. Quads: questions-words.txt (Mikolov et al. 2013, Apache 2.0).

pieces.caption: **Are categories regions, and what is in them?** The section’s three categories, twelve words each: one axis, then a map, then a walk between regions with the real words that live along it, then one point for “bank” and one for “fifth”, and last the test. The regions are real. The interval region is partly a region of ordinals, which is the bank problem inside the section’s own example. Real vectors: 3,146 words of the npm package wink-embeddings-sg-100d 1.1.0 (MIT, GRAYPE Systems), derived from Stanford GloVe pre-trained vectors (PDDL 1.0), inlined. GloVe’s numbers: static, 100 dimensions, not a transformer’s.
